student_notes: Questions from production engineer review. Focus on practical application.

questions.question: The session stores both turn_history and last_3_turns. A user is on turn 8. What does each contain and why are they different sizes?
options: A. Both are identical — turn_history is just the full version of last_3_turns
B. turn_history has all 8 turns in Anthropic format; last_3_turns has only the last 3 turns with bot response text truncated to 400 chars
C. turn_history has the last 20 turns; last_3_turns has the last 3 turns without bot responses
D. turn_history is stored in Postgres; last_3_turns is stored in Redis
questions.explanation: They serve different consumers: turn_history is for the LLM (llm_node), which needs full conversation context to maintain coherence over many turns. last_3_turns is for the SLM classifier (classify_node), which only needs recent context to detect pivots and disambiguation patterns. The SLM has a small context window — feeding it 8 full turns would starve it of room for the taxonomy prompt. The 400-char truncation of bot responses is critical: the SLM needs to know the bot asked 'Shapoorji or Godrej?' (short) but doesn't need the full property carousel description.

questions.question: The Redis optimistic locking uses a separate version key (session:{id}:ver) instead of embedding the version in the session JSON. Why? Under what conditions does this optimization matter most?
questions.answer: The separate version key avoids parsing the full session JSON blob in the Lua script for every save. After turn 20 with full turn_history, the session JSON is 15-20KB. Decoding 20KB of JSON inside a Lua script (which runs on the Redis server's main thread) blocks all other Redis operations for 2-5ms per write. With 10,000 concurrent users each completing a turn every 30 seconds, that's ~333 saves/second × 3ms = nearly continuous Redis blocking. The tiny version key (1-3 bytes, no parsing) makes the CAS check a single GET of a small key. The optimization matters most at high turn counts (turns 15-20, when session JSON is largest) and high concurrency (>1000 sessions active simultaneously).
questions.explanation: This is a micro-optimization that becomes macro-critical at scale. The session JSON growth as turn_history fills is a non-obvious time bomb — it looks fine in testing (turn 2) and degrades gradually in production (turn 10+).
